### An appointment as programme coordinator now actually grants access (2026-08-08)
- `supabase/migrations/20260816020001_programme_coordinator_authz.sql` — **FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated.** The `cohort_coordinators` subsystem (table, audit table, appoint/remove/reinstate/overview RPCs, `fn_is_cohort_coordinator`, the live `trg_cohort_coordinator_on_departure` trigger) has been on production for weeks with **0 appointment rows and ZERO callers of `fn_is_cohort_coordinator` anywhere in the database or the app** — it could record an appointment and nothing consulted it, so an appointment granted nothing. This file recreates none of that; every body starts from its live `pg_get_functiondef` text (dumped 2026-08-08) with only the marked branch added. **No RPC signature changes** (a parallel lane is coding the UI against them). **THE WIRING:** `fn_soi_can_review_applications`, `fn_soi_can_manage_batch` and `fn_soi_has_programme_access` each gain ONE appointment branch **beside** — never replacing — the existing `cohort.manage` / `cohort.school_of_influence.manage` branch (D10), so an appointment alone opens the review queue, the batch screens and module entry with no role grant and no permission key. **D9: that branch carries no institution predicate** — a coordinator decides every applicant to their programme from any college and nothing outside it; `programme_kind` IS the boundary. **D1** widens appoint/remove from `is_super_admin()`-only to admins, the COO (by VALUE via `user_roles`→`custom_roles`, not key existence) and the programme owner, through two new helpers `fn_is_cohort_programme_authority` / `fn_can_appoint_cohort_coordinator`; `fn_cohort_coordinators_overview` is widened to the same three cluster authorities **but deliberately NOT to coordinators** (it returns every programme at once). **D5** adds the additive nullable `cohort_coordinators.may_appoint_others` (DEFAULT true, every reader COALESCEs): a coordinator may appoint, but rows they create are written `false`, capping the chain at one hop by data instead of walking a parent chain that the table has no pointer for. **D13** refuses a manual removal with a blank reason (22023); the departure trigger supplies its own and is untouched. **D6** — nobody marks their own homework — makes `fn_soi_prepare_acceptance` / `fn_soi_confirm_acceptance` / `fn_soi_reject_application` raise 42501 on the caller's own application, **super admins included**. **D11** adds `fn_cohort_coordinator_close_ended_programmes()` (event row written FIRST, then the update — never one `UPDATE … RETURNING` that would be its own only witness); **no cron/vercel entry is created**, a nightly routine should call it. All 12 functions stay SECURITY DEFINER with a pinned `search_path`, and `REVOKE … FROM anon, PUBLIC` is re-asserted on every one (verified: anon holds nothing, before or after).
- ✅ **BEGIN..ROLLBACK rehearsed twice on production, behaviourally — not just "it parses".** Impersonating a real plain learner via `request.jwt.claims`: manage-batch / review / module-entry / can-appoint all **false → true** on the appointment alone, and **false** for a sister programme (D9 boundary holds). One-hop: the appointee's `may_appoint_others` is written **false**, that person then **cannot** appoint but **can** still manage the batch. Blank removal reason → **22023**, with a reason → **true**. Self-review → **42501 on all three** decision RPCs, and again **42501 for a super admin on their own application** while that same super admin reviews other people's fine. D11: **0 closed** while the batches are enrolling, **0 closed** with the intake window 30 days past but the batches `'active'` (in delivery — see the hardening bullet), then **2 closed** once they are `'draft'` with that same past window, the audit rows written, a second run closing **0** (idempotent), and an appointment to `foundations` — a programme with zero cohorts — **kept**, because a programme that never started has not ended. D10 regression: a user with **0 appointments** holding `cohort.manage` still opens both gates. Residue verified in a separate call: 0 coordinator rows, 0 event rows, 0 new functions, no new column on production.
- 🛡️ **Hardened after multi-agent review; four of the findings were real and one was not.** (1) **The owner branch was an escalation path.** Owning ONE batch conferred programme-wide appointment rights, and the appointment branches are institution-free by D9 — so owning a single batch in one college reached every applicant in every college. Now: name a cohort and you must own THAT cohort; appoint programme-wide and you must own **every** non-archived cohort of the kind. Plus a **self-appointment guard** — only a cluster authority (super admin / admin / COO, expressed as the deliberate `fn_is_cohort_programme_authority(NULL, NULL)` call, which returns false for owners because the owner branch needs a programme) may appoint themselves. Proven: owning 1 of 3 → programme-wide **false**, own batch **true**, sister batch **false**; owning all 3 → **true**; a coordinator self-appointing → **42501**. (2) **`hard_deadline`/`closes_at` is the INTAKE window, not programme end** — as originally written D11 stripped every coordinator the day applications closed, mid-delivery, contradicting this same file's `fn_soi_prepare_acceptance` comment. An SoI batch now counts as running while `status IN ('active','enrolling')`; only one still `'draft'` with its window past is ended by the deadline. (3) **A coordinator could remove peers** — including the programme owner's appointee — invisibly, since the overview RPC is closed to coordinators. A non-authority may now only remove appointments where `appointed_by` is themselves. (4) The re-appoint path returned an existing active row untouched, so an admin could never lift a `may_appoint_others=false` set by a coordinator; it now lifts (never lowers) and RAISEs 22023 instead of returning NULL if `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` swallowed some other unique violation. Also: rows are taken `FOR UPDATE` and `status='active'` re-asserted on the update, so the returned count is what was actually ended; `REVOKE UPDATE (may_appoint_others)` from anon+authenticated. **REJECTED — the review asked for `ur.is_active` / `ur.expires_at` / `ur.revoked_at` liveness predicates on the COO join; `user_roles` has none of those columns** (it is `id, user_id, role_id, is_primary, assigned_at, assigned_by`) and the check already matches this repo's own canonical pattern in `fn_is_hr_admin` / `fn_induction_can_manage_coordinators`.
- 🔑 **The rehearsal caught something no review did.** `fn_cohort_coordinator_close_ended_programmes` is maintenance that can mass-remove every appointment in the system, so it is granted to `service_role` only — but the first pass revoked EXECUTE from `anon, PUBLIC` and asserted the result, and the assertion came back **holding**: Supabase's `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` had granted `authenticated` a DIRECT grant that a PUBLIC revoke does not touch. `authenticated` is now named explicitly in that one REVOKE. The standing rule in this repo names anon; this is the same defect one role over.
- ⚠️ **Known and deliberate, stated so it is not discovered later.** A keyless appointed coordinator can open the module, run the batches and READ/REJECT applications, but **cannot yet ACCEPT anyone**: `fn_soi_prepare_acceptance`'s coherence gate still requires `cohort.create` + `cohort.view` + institution access for a non-admin, because the enrolment runs under `cohort_memberships` RLS as the caller and **those policies are not widened here**. Admitting the coordinator in the gate without widening the policies would be strictly worse than the gap — the explicit named refusal would become a bare 42501 from RLS after the reviewer has already picked a batch. Separate reviewed PR. Likewise `fn_cohort_coordinators_overview` admits only cluster authorities, so a programme **owner** may now appoint and remove but cannot read that list (it returns every programme's bench at once, and scoping it per owned kind changes the JSON shape the UI lane is coding against).
- ⚠️ The §0 guard probes `is_admin(uuid)`, not `is_admin()` — it is declared `is_admin(user_id uuid DEFAULT auth.uid())`, so the no-argument form callers write does not name an existing procedure and the guard fired on a healthy database until this was corrected.
- 🛡️ **Second review round — one more real scope gap, and the file is now self-contained for review.** (F1, HIGH) `fn_soi_can_review_applications` is keyed on the **event**, and its queue holds applicants who have **no batch yet** (under `staff_assign` nobody has chosen one), so admitting a BATCH-scoped appointment there handed the holder every applicant of the whole event — other batches, and other colleges wherever batches share a `source_event_id`. The review branch now requires a **programme-wide** appointment (`cohort_id IS NULL`); a batch-scoped appointment still opens module entry and `fn_soi_can_manage_batch` for its own batch, which is batch-keyed and can honour the narrower grant. Proven: batch-scoped → own batch **true**, sister batch **false**, event review **false**, reject **42501**; the same person made programme-wide → review **true**, sister batch **true**. (F4) `fn_cohort_coordinator_remove` now reads `FOR UPDATE` — it races the newly-added nightly auto-close, which also locks — re-asserts `status='active'` on the update and returns `FOUND`, so a double-click yields **true then false with one audit row**, not two contradictory ones. (F6) `programme_kind` is validated against the table's own CHECK list; `''` and an unknown kind raise 22023 instead of writing an active row that matches no cohort. (F3) `REVOKE INSERT (may_appoint_others)` joins the UPDATE revoke — both are **no-ops against today's grants** and are written for the future, because `authenticated` holds `r` and nothing else on this table.
- 📋 **The migration now carries a LIVE BASELINE comment block** — `fn_is_cohort_coordinator`'s full body, `cohort_coordinators`' RLS state, table ACL, all four indexes (including the two partial uniques `appoint()`'s ON CONFLICT depends on) and both CHECK lists, read from production 2026-08-08. None of those objects exist anywhere in this repository, so without it no reviewer can check the deltas against a known baseline. It also records that the LIVE `fn_soi_can_review_applications` already admitted **both** `cohort.manage` and `cohort.school_of_influence.manage` before this file — the repo's last committed copy (`20260808146000_soi_review_accept_queue.sql`) shows one key and is stale, which reads as an un-narrated change to anyone diffing the tree instead of the database.
- 🔒 **`fn_is_cohort_coordinator`'s anon lock is re-asserted here even though this file does not redefine it.** §6 makes it the linchpin of three live gates for the first time — until this PR nothing in the database or the app called it at all — so the function that decides School-of-Influence access is now locked in the same file that gives it that job. No-op against today's grants. It also keeps the `New SECURITY DEFINER functions lock anon` CI gate honest about the LIVE BASELINE block, whose quoted definition the guard's parser reads as real DDL because it does not strip `--` comments; the whole-file `ci:allow-secdef-anon` escape hatch was deliberately NOT used, since weakening a real gate to accommodate a comment is the wrong trade.
### Semester-level timetables were invisible in the unmarked-attendance count — 2026-08-08
- `supabase/migrations/20260816030000_unmarked_periods_regrain_to_timetable.sql` — **FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated.** Re-grains `fn_aqs_attendance_unmarked_periods_today` and `fn_aqs_attendance_faculty_compliance_today` from the SECTION to the TIMETABLE. Both carried `AND t.section_id IS NOT NULL`, and `timetables.section_id` is nullable: 60 of 195 active timetables leave it NULL because they are semester-level (one timetable for a whole semester rather than one per section). Every one of them was missing from the attention-bar pending badge and from the HOD compliance figure. Measured live on a Saturday: **29 real teaching sessions invisible**, among them II M.Com, II MBA, II B.Sc (Mathematics), II M.Sc Zoology and III B.A History. Bodies start VERBATIM from production `pg_get_functiondef` (2026-08-08); the repository copy in `attention_bar_state_query_functions_v1.sql` matched the live definition apart from comments, so the stale-body trap was checked and clear. That predecessor file is deliberately left untouched — this repository corrects a migration with a new one rather than editing a shipped file.
- 🛑 **DELETING THE PREDICATE ON ITS OWN IS THE HARMFUL FIX, AND THIS IS THE ENTIRE POINT OF THE CHANGE.** Three mechanisms, all measured rather than argued. (1) The aggregate was `COUNT(DISTINCT t.section_id)` and `COUNT(DISTINCT)` discards NULLs by definition — on production the same day, the shipped count and the naive-fix count were **both 85** while the underlying row set grew from 85 to 128; forty-three extra rows, every one swallowed by the aggregate. (2) `ARRAY(SELECT DISTINCT t2.section_id ...)` starts emitting NULL elements into `sample_period_ids`. (3) The killer: the clearing test was `NOT EXISTS (... sa.section_id = t.section_id)`, and with `t.section_id` NULL that comparison is NULL, never TRUE, so `NOT EXISTS` is **always** true and the row reports itself unmarked **forever — including after somebody marks it**. Not hypothetical: two semester-level timetables had already been marked that day and the naive shape still called both unmarked. A one-line fix would therefore have moved the number by zero and manufactured to-dos nobody could ever clear.
- 🔑 **The fix is one grain shared by the counting key and the clearing key.** `COUNT(DISTINCT t.section_id)` → `COUNT(DISTINCT t.id)`; `SELECT DISTINCT t2.section_id` → `SELECT DISTINCT t2.id`; `section_id IS NOT NULL` → `NOT COALESCE(is_template, false)`; and `sa.section_id = t.section_id` → `sa.timetable_id = t.id`. `student_attendance.timetable_id` is **NOT NULL** (verified live: 11,120 rows, 0 nulls), so the existence key is total and mechanism 3 has no NULL hole to reopen. Because both keys now name the same column, whatever is counted can be cleared — by construction, not by care.
- ⚠️ **The template filter is not optional and not tidying.** 19 of the 60 active semester-level rows are templates and 12 of them listed that day; dropping the section predicate without adding `NOT is_template` injects a dozen teaching sessions that do not exist. It also corrects a pre-existing defect — the shipped count already included 1 template.
- 📐 **Measured impact, and the arithmetic closes exactly.** 85 → 114 at super-admin scope: **−1** template that should never have been counted, **+29** semester-level timetables that were invisible, **+1** section-level timetable that the tighter existence key correctly no longer clears (a SIBLING timetable in the same section had been clearing it). Re-measure before relying on any of these — roughly nine sessions write this database concurrently, and these numbers were **already stale 40 minutes later the same morning** (re-read: 81 → 110). The DIFFERENCE held exactly — +29, −1, +1 — and so did every relationship, which is why the suite asserts relationships and never a literal count. Magnitude of the blind spot: semester-level timetables hold **3,946 attendance rows across 195 distinct timetables and 246 distinct days**, from 2025-09-04 to 2026-08-08 — about 35% of every attendance row on the platform — and all 3,946 store a non-NULL `student_attendance.section_id` while their own `section_id` is NULL, which is precisely why the old section-to-section key could never match one.
- 🔁 **The sibling is fixed in the same file on purpose.** `fn_aqs_attendance_faculty_compliance_today` carried the identical predicate; both numbers render on `/academic/attendance/dashboard`, so correcting one alone would have left the compliance figure visibly contradicting the pending figure. Return shapes are unchanged — the JSON keys `count`, `sample_period_ids`, `total_faculty`, `compliant_count`, `non_compliant_count`, `non_compliant_user_ids` are addressed by name in `quick_action_rules.when_clause`. Only the MEANING of the two id arrays changes: timetable UUIDs, no longer section UUIDs. Verified by grep that no TypeScript reads either array.
- 📝 **Registry copy ships with it, because the counting unit changed.** Two `quick_action_state_queries` descriptions and both badge labels on `quick_action_rules` (`…000004` for the Senior Learner, `…000003` for the HOD) said "sections"; they now say sessions, set with `jsonb_set` so `href`/`cta`/`icon` survive. Both UPDATE blocks are idempotent and guarded with `to_regclass`, since a fresh environment may not have seeded the registry.
- 🔒 `REVOKE EXECUTE … FROM anon, PUBLIC` re-asserted on both functions alongside `GRANT … TO authenticated, service_role`, matching the live ACL. Neither had an anon grant before and neither has one after; the revoke is the guarantee, not a repair.
- 🧪 **Proved behaviourally, and the proof is proved.** `__tests__/academic/unmarked-periods-timetable-grain.test.ts` applies the migration VERBATIM to a real PostgreSQL, seeds an estate and reads back what the database actually did — it never re-implements the query in TypeScript. The headline assertion is a **disappearance**, not a count: mark a semester-level timetable and it must leave the result, which is the only test that exercises mechanism 3. No literal production count is asserted anywhere; every assertion is a relationship (before/after, subset, distinctness) against a fixture the file created. 17 assertions, proved non-vacuous by four mutants: reverting the existence key to `section_id` kills 3 (including the headline), dropping the template filter kills 2, reverting to the section grain kills 3, and removing the anon revokes kills 2. Requires a local PostgreSQL and is deliberately loud rather than skipped; CI runs only three named vitest files, so this path is not in the CI build.
- 🕳️ **A SECOND column reopened the same hole, and review caught it.** The first draft kept the inherited `AND (v_institution_id IS NULL OR sa.institution_id = v_institution_id)` inside the `NOT EXISTS`. That filters timetables on `t.institution_id` but tests attendance on `sa.institution_id` — **different columns**. Any attendance row whose denormalised institution drifts from its timetable's satisfies the count side and fails the existence test, so for an institution-scoped caller that session reads unmarked forever after being marked: mechanism 3, reopened through a second column, in the very change that exists to close it. Production already holds **1 such row** (measured). The predicate was also redundant — `sa.timetable_id = t.id` pins exactly one timetable and `t` is already institution-scoped, so it could only ever wrongly EXCLUDE a match. Removed from both functions, with a comment saying not to add it back, and pinned by a fixture whose attendance row names a different institution than its timetable.
- 🔍 **The mutation run found a gap in the tests themselves.** Reintroducing the asymmetric predicate on the OUTER query alone did not fail anything at first: the assertions checked `sample_period_ids`, which is built by a **separate copy** of the predicate list in the `ARRAY(... t2 ...)` subquery, and the one count-consistency assertion ran only at super-admin scope where a NULL `v_institution_id` makes the clause inert. Two hand-maintained copies of one predicate list can drift, and a drift renders as a badge number that disagrees with the list behind it. The suite now asserts `count = distinct ids` at **both** an unscoped and an institution-scoped caller, which kills the outer-only mutant.
- 🚩 **OPEN, DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED HERE — a Director decision.** `lib/services/academic/attendance-dashboard-service.ts:384` filters weekends out of its date range; the RPC does not. The disagreement already exists (the badge shows a number while a Saturday list renders empty) and this change WIDENS it, because JKKN demonstrably teaches on Saturdays — **133 active timetables list SATURDAY**. Either the RPC learns to skip weekends or the dashboard learns to honour Saturday. Whichever way it goes, one of the two is currently lying to a Senior Learner.
- 🔒 **CLOSED IN THIS FILE — three guards, added because the re-grain widened what was leaking (85 → 114 ids, now including the formerly-hidden semester rows).** The inherited shape took *both* identity and scope from caller-supplied arguments on a `SECURITY DEFINER` function granted to every signed-in user. Three rounds of review found three distinct holes, each fixed here and each proven by mutation (remove the guard, the assertion fails):
  1. **Identity guard** (both functions) — `p_user_id` was never compared to `auth.uid()`, so any signed-in caller could name a super administrator and have the clamp faithfully evaluate *that* person's privileges. Both functions now return an empty result when `auth.uid()` is present and names someone else. Service-role and internal callers are unaffected by construction: `auth.uid()` is NULL for them, so the guard does not fire and `p_user_id` is honoured as before. The app is on the guarded path — `lib/attention-bar/state-queries.ts` uses `createServerSupabaseClient()`, the cookie-backed session client.
  2. **Institution clamp** — `p_institution_id` overrode scope with no authorization gate. Only a genuinely cluster-scoped caller may now redirect it; everyone else keeps their own profile's institution whatever they pass. Scope is read from **`custom_roles.institution_scope`**, not a hardcoded role-name list. That distinction is load-bearing and was itself a review finding: production holds **no `custom_roles` row named `admin`** yet one live profile still carries that legacy value (institution-scoped, unflagged), while the two real `administrator` users are cluster-scoped *without* the `is_super_admin` flag and with no `institution_id`. A name list gets one of those two wrong in whichever direction it is written.
  3. **Fail-closed on NULL scope** — the predicate reads a NULL institution as CLUSTER-WIDE, not "none", so a non-cluster caller whose institution cannot be resolved used to fall through into every college's data. It now returns empty.
  Also fixed: department resolution is skipped for cluster-scoped callers, who would otherwise have their cluster view silently collapsed to one department by an incidental `staff` row (fails safe, but under-reports).
  **Verified against the live catalog, not against schema files:** a review finding proposed filtering the role lookup by `custom_roles.institution_id` on the grounds that the table is keyed `(institution_id, role_key)`. Production has **no `institution_id` column** on `custom_roles` and `role_key` is UNIQUE on its own (88 roles, 88 distinct keys), so no per-tenant collision is possible and that filter would have referenced a column that does not exist. The claim came from a migration file; the catalog disagrees.
  **Still open here, deliberately:** the sibling `fn_aqs_*` functions in the original file (billing, counselor, admission) carry the same argument-derived-identity shape and are untouched — worth a family-wide sweep in its own change.
- 📏 **KNOWN AND ACCEPTED: the grain is per timetable per day, not per period.** A timetable can hold several periods in one day (production maximum observed: 6 attendance rows for one timetable on one date), and a single row for today clears the whole timetable — so a query named `unmarked_periods` still under-counts a partially-marked day. This is **inherited, and strictly tighter than what shipped** (the old key cleared on any row for the whole *section*, across every timetable in it). Moving to a true period grain needs a period key on both sides and is a separate change.
- ✅ **Refuted during review, with evidence:** a concern that nullable `timetables.department_id` would still hide semester-level rows from HOD scope does not hold — **0 of the 60** active semester-level rows have a NULL department, and 0 section-level rows do either.
- 🪞 **The non-vacuity proof had itself gone vacuous, and review caught that too.** Adding the institution-mismatch fixture in round 1 marked it against `SEC_1` — and because the section-keyed CONTROLS carry no institution or department filter, that one row cleared every `SEC_1` timetable for them as well. `fn_ctl_orig_unmarked()` was returning **count 0 with an empty array**, so `expect(naive.count).toBe(orig.count)` was asserting `0 === 0` and every control `not.toContain(...)` was passing against nothing. Confirmed by reverting the single section id: two assertions fail with *expected 0 to be greater than 0*. The fixture now marks its own `SEC_3`, and a **guard test** asserts the control returns a non-empty set (`count > 0` and `SEC_1` present) before any comparison runs — a control that returns the empty set can refute nothing, and this class of rot is silent.
- ⚛️ **The file is now one transaction, and that is proven, not assumed.** `BEGIN;` / `COMMIT;` wrap both functions and the registry copy. The concern is specific: a missing `anon` / `authenticated` / `service_role` role in some environment aborts the run *between* the two `CREATE OR REPLACE` statements, leaving function 1 on the timetable grain and function 2 on sections — the pending figure and the compliance figure disagreeing on one screen, which is the exact split this file exists to prevent. Proved by injecting a failing statement before `COMMIT` against a scratch database: function 1 is absent afterwards, so nothing partial survives.
- ⚠️ **KNOWN AND DISCLOSED — this fix is an improvement, not a completion.** A semester-level timetable spans several sections, and the existence key is the timetable, so marking ONE section clears the whole row while the others stay unmarked and invisible. Measured: **307 of 3,419** semester-timetable-days carry more than one section, up to **6** sections on a single timetable in one day. This is not a regression — those rows were counted **zero** times before — but it is the next step, and it needs an expected-section list per timetable, which the timetable row does not carry (its `section_id` is NULL by definition). Same shape as the per-period gap above.
- 🕰️ **Also inherited, also not fixed:** `CURRENT_DATE` and `TO_CHAR(CURRENT_DATE,'DAY')` resolve in the session timezone with no pin, so a UTC session between 00:00 and 05:30 IST evaluates yesterday. Affects the old and new shapes identically; a timezone pin changes what "today" means for every caller and belongs to its own reviewed change.
### How many classes were marked the same day — the detector for a lesson gate, 2026-08-08
- `supabase/migrations/20260816020000_work_signal_marked_same_day.sql` — **APPLIED to production 2026-08-08** by the Director, shortly after #2924 merged. ⚠️ **This entry originally read "FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated" and that is no longer true** — verified live the same day: `fn_try_timestamptz_ist` exists, the `sessions_marked_same_day` registry row exists, the engine body contains `v_personal_same_day`, and the live RPC returns the chip. **The version that was applied is the one #2924 merged, which still carries the four raising inputs corrected below** — the fixes were still in review when it merged and landed separately; the file in this repo is the corrected one, so re-applying it is the intended remedy and the §0 guard makes that a safe no-op-or-upgrade. Adds one work signal, `sessions_marked_same_day`, and shipped DELIBERATELY BEFORE the lesson gate it exists to measure, because a before/after reading needs the before. `fn_work_signals_for` derives every marking number from `sa.attendance_date` alone, so a class marked twenty-one days late is today indistinguishable from one marked in the room; nothing anywhere measures the lag between a class and the act of recording it. **The obvious column is the wrong one:** `student_attendance` holds one row per day per section with the day's periods packed into `attendance_data` (~2.74 periods per row, measured 2026-08-08), so `created_at` belongs to whichever period was inserted first and every later period inherits its punctual timestamp; `updated_at` is client-supplied and a live row was observed where it PRECEDES `created_at`. The correct source is per-period `marked_by_details.marked_at`, the natural partner of the `marker_id` this function already reads — and the repo knew it: `20260722160000_att_reconcile_v2` line 30 says the marking timestamp is `marked_at` "(NOT the row created_at)".
- 🔴 **It also documents a bug that is already live.** Signals are emitted by an INNER JOIN of `work_signal_types` against an inline VALUES list, so a key registered without a VALUES row is silently dropped — no error, no chip. Verified on production 2026-08-08: **14 active registry rows, 13 VALUES rows**; `marks_coverage` has been registered since `20260717170852` and has never had an emitter, so it has been dark its whole life. The existing SQL battery could not see it because that battery asserts a HARDCODED key list, which can only ever confirm the keys someone remembered to write down. `__tests__/work-signals/registry-values-parity.test.ts` now derives both sides from the migrations and fails on any registered-but-unemitted key, with `marks_coverage` pinned as the one known gap so a future fix must shrink that list deliberately. **This file adds both halves for its own key.** `marks_coverage` is NOT fixed here — it needs a real ratio computation, which is a separate decision.
- 🕐 **`AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'` is load-bearing, not decoration.** Measured on production over the trailing 30 days: IST reads **6,651** same-day periods, UTC reads **6,673** — they disagree on 22. (An earlier reading found them equal; that was a coincidence of marking hours and has already stopped being true.) `attendance_date` is an IST calendar date, so truncating a UTC instant credits a class marked at 02:30 IST to the previous day.
- 🛡️ **The cast cannot raise — and TWO drafts got there by enumerating, which is the wrong shape of rule.** **CORRECTED 2026-08-08 after #2924 merged; see #FOLLOWUP.** `marked_at` is client-written text inside jsonb. Across all **31,037** attributable periods there are zero empty strings and zero non-ISO values, so none of this changes a number today — but **1,028** of those periods carry a `marker_id` with no `marked_at` at all, proving the field is not written by every path. One malformed value would make a bare `::timestamptz` RAISE; `WorkSignalsService` resolves any error to null and the card renders nothing on null, so a single poisoned string would silently blank My Pulse. **Draft 1** used `~ '^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}'` and claimed that made a raise impossible — false and withdrawn: a prefix regex tests SHAPE, not VALIDITY, and `2026-13-40` / `2026-02-30` / `0000-00-00` all satisfy it and raise **22008** (verified). **Draft 2 — the version that merged in #2924** — trapped 22007 + 22008 by name; review then found `+99:00` raises **22009** and a misspelt zone (`Asia/Kolkatta`) raises **22023**, both escaping (verified on production). A list extended in two consecutive rounds is not a rule. The shipped `fn_try_ist_date` swallows **class 22 (data exception) and re-raises everything else** — complete by the standard's own definition, and the re-raise covers everything `OTHERS` genuinely catches — SQLSTATE 53 (resources), 40 (deadlock/serialization) and 58/XX — so a real failure never becomes "not marked that day". ⚠️ An earlier version of this entry credited the re-raise with protecting 57014 `query_canceled`; that was wrong and is corrected — verified on production, plpgsql's `OTHERS` already excludes `QUERY_CANCELED`, so a statement timeout propagates on its own.
- 🕰️ **The helper returns a DATE, not an instant, and the naive branch is strict.** Returning the instant left `… AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date` at the call site — datetime arithmetic on client text **outside** the trap — so `294276-12-31T23:59:59Z` parsed cleanly and then overflowed on the +05:30 shift, raising in the engine. Every failing step now happens behind the handler. And the zone-free test is anchored: draft 2's "does this look zoned?" check sent anything it failed to recognise to `::timestamp`, which **silently discards** the zone — verified on production, `…T20:00:00z` (lowercase), `…T23:50:00+05` (two-digit offset) and `2026-08-07 23:00:00 UTC` all lost their zone and were re-anchored as IST wall-clock, a 5.5-hour shift that moves the calendar day at exactly the late-evening boundary the branch exists to get right. Doubtful values now take the SAFE path, not the lossy one. ⚠️ **The zone-free test errs in BOTH directions if you let it, and a first correction over-tightened:** an exact-width, untrimmed pattern REJECTED genuinely zone-free values it merely failed to recognise, so `2026-08-08 23:30:00 ` (trailing space) and `2026-8-8 23:30:00` fell to the zoned branch, were read in the session zone (UTC) and landed a day late — a regression against the version already running. The shipped test `btrim`s first and accepts 1-2 digit month/day/hour. Being unrecognised must not silently mean "assume UTC".
- ⚙️ **Scope is settled by query shape, not by the planner.** The marker test is in the WHERE and the day test in an aggregate FILTER, and FILTER only sees rows the WHERE admitted — so another marker's poisoned row can never be parsed on this caller's behalf, and `same_day <= personally-marked` holds because a FILTER count cannot exceed the count it filters. Both counters come from ONE scan instead of two. Helper cost measured rather than assumed: the busiest single marker has **701** periods across ALL time (mean 94 over 329 markers), so the per-row subtransaction is bounded well inside the 20s `statement_timeout`.
- 🔁 **The file is ONE TRANSACTION, and that is what makes §0 a guard at all.** A `RAISE` inside a standalone `DO` aborts that block — it does NOT stop the next statement from being pasted and run, and this file reaches the database out-of-band, statement by statement. Un-wrapped, §0 could refuse and the `CREATE OR REPLACE` could still overwrite a drifted engine a moment later. Explicit `BEGIN;`/`COMMIT;`; strip them only if your apply path already opens a transaction. The retire block additionally pairs its check and its `EXECUTE DROP` inside one `DO`, **counts remaining callers and REFUSES while any exist** (a plpgsql body is stored as TEXT so Postgres records no dependency — a bare `DROP` would succeed while the live engine still called it, and My Pulse would go blank), and filters `prokind IN ('f','p')` because `pg_get_functiondef` raises **42809** on aggregates and window functions and would otherwise abort the retire the day an extension adds one.
- 🚧 **§0 drift guard — it REFUSES to apply on a body it did not read.** This file rewrites the whole ~7,027-char engine from a 2026-08-08 snapshot, but the apply is Director-gated to an unknown later date, six migrations define this function, and DDL reaches production out-of-band. Applying stale weeks later would silently revert whatever shipped in between. The guard proceeds only if the live body is the snapshot (`md5 09432834a331932fbae2d5a90d607d12`) **or** already contains `v_personal_same_day` (making a re-run a no-op); anything else RAISES `REFUSING TO APPLY` with the live md5 and length.
- 🔢 **5.9% is UNKNOWN, not late.** 526 of 8,896 periods in the trailing 30 days carry no `marked_by_details` at all, spanning 2025-07-09 to 2026-08-07 — an ACTIVE second write path, not legacy residue. They are already excluded from the personally-marked count so the two counters stay consistent, but the label counts a positive act and makes no claim about the remainder. Nothing here may be read as an accusation.
- ⚠️ **Two live definitions of "on time" now exist** — `fn_att_reconcile_propose` counts on-time as within 15 minutes of period start, this counts the calendar day, so a person can be green here and late there. Flagged for a deliberate decision, NOT resolved. ⚠️ **Read the new chip against the small "you:" number, not the big one** — `sessions_marked`'s headline is the ASSIGNED count while this counts what the caller personally marked, so side by side it looks smaller for reasons unrelated to timeliness. `sort_order` 11 places it directly beside `sessions_marked` for exactly that reason.
- 🔒 Body reproduced VERBATIM from `pg_get_functiondef` on production 2026-08-08 (verified byte-identical, 7027 chars, to `20260731190000` — six files define this function and the newest is not automatically what runs). SECURITY DEFINER; anon+PUBLIC EXECUTE revoked and `authenticated`+`service_role` re-granted in the same file, and the same lock applied to the new `fn_try_ist_date` (which is NOT SECURITY DEFINER — it reads nothing). **No UI change:** `work-signals-card.tsx` renders `value`/`label`/`action_route` straight from the registry with no hardcoded map, confirmed by reading it. `.claude/battery-two-sided-close.sql` A10b skips when the key is **not registered** — gating the skip on the REGISTRY rather than on the RPC response is deliberate, because probing the response makes "never applied" and "registered but dropped by the inner join" indistinguishable, which would let a typo'd VALUES row print "skipped" and pass, reproducing `marks_coverage` exactly. Suite proven non-vacuous by **26 mutants, all killed**, across five rounds — two mutants survived earlier rounds and both exposed real holes: a second scan comma-joined into the same FROM clause slipped past a `FROM …` occurrence count, the block-extraction regex was matching the *earlier* assigned/witnessed aggregate so the scoping assertion graded the wrong FILTER (and, separately, compared two offsets in an order valid SQL can never violate — grammar, not scoping), and two later fixes shipped with no assertion at all until a mutant found them.
- 🔒 Body reproduced VERBATIM from `pg_get_functiondef` on production 2026-08-08 (verified byte-identical, 7027 chars, to `20260731190000` — six files define this function and the newest is not automatically what runs). SECURITY DEFINER; anon+PUBLIC EXECUTE revoked and `authenticated`+`service_role` re-granted in the same file, and the same lock applied to the new `fn_try_timestamptz_ist` (which is NOT SECURITY DEFINER — it reads nothing). **No UI change:** `work-signals-card.tsx` renders `value`/`label`/`action_route` straight from the registry with no hardcoded map, confirmed by reading it. `.claude/battery-two-sided-close.sql` A10b probes for the new key rather than requiring it, because this migration is not applied and a battery that fails on a database lacking it would be testing the deployment rather than the behaviour. Suite proven non-vacuous by **12 mutants, all killed** — including a first round where one survived (a second scan comma-joined into the same FROM clause slipped past a `FROM …` count) and the assertion was tightened to count the table.

### The rest of the fn_aqs_* family still took its identity from an argument, 2026-08-08
- `supabase/migrations/20260817010000_aqs_family_identity_and_scope_guards.sql` — **FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated.** `20260816030000` hardened two members of this family against three holes that all follow from one shape: a SECURITY DEFINER function GRANTed to `authenticated` that takes BOTH its identity (`p_user_id`) and its scope (`p_institution_id`) as ARGUMENTS. The other three were never audited. All five live bodies were read from `pg_get_functiondef` on production and classified; the verdicts differ, and only what is genuinely exposed is touched. `fn_aqs_billing_overdue_invoices` was exposed on all three and is fixed for all three. `fn_aqs_counselor_pending_leads` was exposed on identity ONLY — it takes no institution argument and already returns `count 0` when the caller owns no counselor record — so it gets the identity guard and nothing else. `fn_aqs_admission_leads_unassigned_count` was **already safe on identity** and is documented as such rather than "fixed": it has no `p_user_id` and derives the caller from `auth.uid()`, which is the shape the other four should have had. The two attendance functions are deliberately NOT re-created here — re-shipping a hardened body from a second file is how it gets silently reverted.
- 🔓 **The identity hole was the severe one, and it was not theoretical.** Any of the **7,236** profiles could sign in and name a super administrator through PostgREST; the function then faithfully evaluated THAT person's privileges. On billing that returned the cluster-wide overdue count, the total overdue amount and the age of the oldest unpaid bill. On `fn_aqs_counselor_pending_leads` it returned more than a figure — the oldest pending lead's UUID, its age, **and the applicant's full name** — so naming another counselor handed over an identified individual. The guard refuses only when `auth.uid()` IS NOT NULL and names someone else, so `service_role` and internal contexts (where `auth.uid()` is NULL and full trust already applies) keep working; the app itself is on the guarded path because `lib/attention-bar/state-queries.ts` builds its client with `createServerSupabaseClient()`, the cookie-backed session client.
- 🚫 **The role-name list was wrong in BOTH directions, and a test proves it rather than asserting it.** The shipped bodies decided cluster scope with literals — `v_user_role IN ('super_admin','admin')`, plus `'admission'` in the admission counter. Measured on production 2026-08-08: `custom_roles` holds **NO row named `admin`** at all, yet **one** live profile still carries the legacy value `role='admin'` WITH an `institution_id` and WITHOUT the `is_super_admin` flag — the list handed that single-tenant user the entire cluster's billing position. In the other direction the **2** real `administrator` users ARE `institution_scope='all'` but are NOT flagged and hold NO `institution_id`, so clamping on the flag alone would have emptied their screen instead. Scope is therefore read from `custom_roles.institution_scope`, which is what Role Management writes and what `role_has_institution_access()` reads (via `user_roles`, and via the same legacy `profiles.role → custom_roles.role_key` fallback used here). Re-verified live rather than inherited: `custom_roles` has **no `institution_id` column** and `role_key` is unique on its own (88 roles, 88 distinct keys), so this lookup needs no further qualification. Restoring the literal in a mutation run fails three tests at once, two of them in opposite directions — `expected 4 to be 2` (over-grant) beside `expected +0 to be 4` (empty screen).
- ⚠️ **DISCLOSED, AND THE ONE THING A REVIEWER MUST ACTIVELY ACCEPT: reading the registry WIDENS who sees cluster-wide billing, from 31 profiles to 138 — 114 gain it, 7 lose it.** The gainers are roles Role Management has already marked `institution_scope='all'`, including `staff_counselor` (46) and `admission_counselor` (31); every one of them already passes `role_has_institution_access()` for any institution, so this aligns the counter with the platform's own answer rather than granting anything new at the policy layer. It is nonetheless a real change in what those people see on screen, and it is larger in practice than the holes closed for billing (which needed either impersonation or a NULL institution). It is also not novel — `20260816030000` made exactly this substitution for the attendance pair and is already live. Flagged because these functions are SECURITY DEFINER and so consult scope WITHOUT consulting `user_has_permission`; if the Director wants billing figures gated on a billing permission as well, that is a separate deliberate change across the whole family, not something to smuggle in beside a security fix.
- 🕳️ **The fail-open was reachable without any impersonation at all.** The scope predicate reads `(v_institution_id IS NULL OR …institution_id = v_institution_id)`, so a NULL institution means CLUSTER-WIDE, not "none". In billing, a `p_user_id` matching **no profile row** left every local flag NULL, skipped both branches, and fell straight through — a random UUID returned the whole cluster's billing position. **16** live profiles (non-super-admin, NULL `institution_id`) reached the same state as themselves. Both now return zero. The `auth.uid() IS NULL` branch in the admission counter is preserved deliberately: unlike its siblings that function has no `p_user_id` to fall back on, so failing closed there would break internal callers that legitimately read the cluster-wide figure.
- 🧪 **Non-vacuity is proved twice over, because a test that also passes against the vulnerable code proves nothing.** `__tests__/attention-bar/aqs-family-identity-guard.test.ts` applies the migration VERBATIM off disk and never re-implements a scope decision in TypeScript. It carries three CONTROL functions reproducing the PRE-FIX bodies exactly as they ran on production, so every "the guard refuses" assertion is paired with a control showing the old shape ANSWERS against the SAME fixture — including one that returns the other counselor's applicant by name. Separately, each of the three guards was mutated out of the real file and the suite re-run: identity removed → 1 failure (`expected 4 to be +0`); registry replaced by the name list → 3 failures in both directions; fail-closed removed → 2 failures. The file was then restored and verified byte-identical (`git diff` empty, zero `MUTATION-TEST` leftovers) and 22/22 pass. Every zero assertion is paired with a non-zero reading of the same value under a legitimate caller, and two fixture-integrity tests assert cluster (4 bills / 5 leads) is strictly greater than one college (2 / 2) before any scope claim runs — a fixture that cannot tell them apart would let every scope test pass vacuously.
- 🔒 All three functions re-assert `REVOKE EXECUTE … FROM anon, PUBLIC` and re-`GRANT` to `authenticated, service_role` in the same file. `anon` is already false for all five on production (the `20260605191101` sweep), so this changes nothing today and exists so a replay on a fresh database cannot inherit Supabase's default `anon` grant. No UI, service or route file is touched — `lib/attention-bar/state-queries.ts` passes the same argument shapes and needs no change.
- 🔁 **REVISED after review — reading only `profiles.role` was the SAME mistake one level down, and the first draft made it.** The initial version inlined `custom_roles cr WHERE cr.role_key = v_role` into two bodies and called it parity with `role_has_institution_access()`. It is not: that function consults **`user_roles` FIRST** — the many-to-many table Role Management actually writes — and falls back to the denormalised `profiles.role` only afterwards. Measured on production: **161** profiles are cluster-scoped via `user_roles` against **138** via `profiles.role`, and **29** are visible ONLY through `user_roles`. Those 29 would have been clamped to a single college — and any of them carrying a NULL institution would have been dropped into the new fail-closed branch and shown a permanent zero, the exact empty-screen regression this file claims to avoid (0 are in that state today, which is luck, not design). Scope now goes through one `fn_aqs_caller_is_cluster_scoped(uuid)` helper that ORs both paths in the same order as the authority — a FUNCTION rather than a third and fourth inlined copy, because "a second copy of a decision is free to drift" is this file's own argument and it applies to itself. The helper is **not** granted to `authenticated` (its SECURITY DEFINER callers execute as owner and need no grant), so it does not become a new argument-takes-identity surface.
- 🧾 **Review claims settled by measurement rather than argument.** `custom_roles.is_active` **exists and is NOT NULL DEFAULT true** on production, so the `AND cr.is_active` filter can neither raise 42703 nor be silently demoted by a NULL; `institution_scope` **is** nullable (default `'own'`), which is why every read is COALESCE-wrapped so a NULL resolves to "not cluster-scoped". **Not fixed, and inherited rather than introduced:** 6 profiles are cluster-scoped through `profiles.role` alone with no `user_roles` row — deleting a role does not clear `profiles.role`, so some are plausibly demoted people still holding the cluster. That over-grant lives in `role_has_institution_access()` itself; this file matches the authority instead of quietly diverging from it.
- 🧪 **Two real vacuity gaps in the first suite, both closed.** (a) The clamp on `fn_aqs_admission_leads_unassigned_count` was only ever exercised with a NULL argument, so deleting `ELSE v_institution_id := v_caller_inst_id` would have left every test green while re-opening cross-tenant redirect. (b) INST and OTHER_INST each held exactly 2 overdue bills, making `expect(redirected.count).toBe(2)` pass whether the clamp held or redirected — vacuity by fixture, in the file that claims its fixture can refute. The estate is now deliberately asymmetric (2 bills vs 3, 2 unassigned leads vs 3) so each count assertion refutes on its own. **One proposed control was itself wrong and the run caught it:** the pre-fix admission body clamped ordinary callers correctly too, so a control expecting it to leak 3 failed with `expected 2 to be 3` — that function's holes were the name list and the fail-open, never argument-redirect. The control is now a super administrator reading the true figure.
- 🔬 **Five mutants, all killed** (28 tests). Identity guard deleted → 1 failure; registry read → name list → 3 failures in **both** directions (`expected 4 to be 2` over-grant beside `expected +0 to be 4` empty screen); fail-closed deleted → 2 failures; `user_roles` branch deleted → 3 failures (`expected 2 to be 5`); `is_active` filter deleted → 1 failure (a deactivated role still granting the cluster). File restored and verified byte-identical after each.
- 📌 **The disclosed widening is now PINNED BY A TEST, not just prose.** A `staff_counselor` fixture (institution_scope='all', 46 holders live) asserts it reads every college's overdue position, with a pre-fix control showing it previously saw only its own — so the 31→138 change is a decision on the record that fails loudly if someone alters it, rather than an emergent behaviour buried in a header. **Deliberately NOT gated on `user_has_permission`:** these functions are SECURITY DEFINER and consult scope without any permission half, which is a pre-existing property of the whole family; adding a permission gate to billing alone would make the five siblings disagree, and it is the Director's call across all of them.
- 🔴💰 **A SEPARATE LIVE DEFECT SURFACED WHILE DOING THIS, AND IS DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED HERE: `total_overdue_amount` returns ₹0 on production, always.** The field sums `final_amount - COALESCE(balance_amount, 0)` — the amount already SETTLED, not the amount owed. The repo's own billing code defines outstanding the other way (`SUM(balance_amount) WHERE balance_amount > 0`, `supabase/setup/02_functions.sql`), and on an unpaid bill `balance_amount` equals `final_amount`, so the subtraction collapses to zero. Measured 2026-08-08: **2,920 overdue bills; this formula returns ₹0.00; the amount actually owed is ₹26,01,97,825.** The attention bar's overdue-amount figure has therefore been ₹0 for every viewer since it shipped — which also means the "cluster-wide financial exposure" the widening debate is about currently discloses a zero. Reproduced verbatim from the live body and RETAINED, because correcting a money figure moves a number on a finance screen and deserves its own review rather than riding along inside an access-control fix; the migration header carries the one-query reproduction. **Raised as its own Director item.**
- 🧾🔍 **Every production number in the header is now reproducible from the header itself.** Review's fair objection was that the safety case rested on statistics a reviewer cannot see in the diff, wrapped in language ("need not be re-litigated") that reads as pre-settling the argument. Three read-only queries are now inlined — cluster-scope by path (161/138/29/6), the name-list-vs-registry table per live role, and the 31→138 widening — so the comment can be checked and contradicted rather than believed. The phrasing was softened accordingly: a comment is not evidence, and nine sessions write this database concurrently, so any figure in it is a measurement with a timestamp, not a fact.
- ⚠️🛑 **The file now carries its own apply-gate.** The widening is stated in the migration header as a decision requiring ratification, not merely disclosed in the PR body — the PR body does not travel with the file, and a future session reading only `supabase/migrations/` would otherwise see a security fix and no mention that applying it hands 114 more people cluster-wide billing.
### Learners Council broadcast approval — one named approver, 24h auto-send, 2026-08-08
- `supabase/migrations/20260808214500_lc_broadcast_approval.sql` — **FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated.** Adds `lc_broadcast_requests` (holding table) + `fn_lc_broadcast_submit` / `fn_lc_broadcast_decide` / `fn_lc_broadcast_cancel` (authenticated) + `fn_lc_broadcast_autosend` (service_role only, driven by `/api/cron/lc-broadcast-autosend`). Two config rows: `lc.broadcast.approver_user_id` (null until named) and `lc.broadcast.auto_send_hours` (24).
- 🚦 **Own-college sends immediately; all-college waits.** Only all-college requests reach the holding table — an own-college message becomes a `notifications` row inside the submit RPC and never queues.
- ⏰ **Silence counts as approval, deliberately.** After `auto_send_hours` the sweep sends the message anyway. The Director chose this on a question that named the consequence in those words; it is a decision, not an oversight. Reverting it is a one-line change in `fn_lc_broadcast_autosend`.
- 🧱 **Why a holding table and not a "pending" notification.** `notifications` carries 261,959 rows with **zero** `sent_at IS NULL`, and nothing in the read path filters on `sent_at` — delivery resolves purely from `targeting`. A row parked there would reach learners immediately, so pending state cannot live in that table.
- 🔒 **Writes go only through the RPCs.** The table has a SELECT policy (own requests, or the named approver, or an admin) and deliberately **no INSERT/UPDATE policy**. `REVOKE ALL … FROM anon, PUBLIC` runs before the grant, because a new table inherits Supabase's default privileges and a bare GRANT afterwards is a no-op.
- 🛡️ **The learners-only rule is enforced twice** — at submit, and again inside the auto-send sweep, in case the council roster or audience changed while a request sat waiting. The sweep is advisory-locked and uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so two overlapping runs cannot double-send.
- 🗣️ **A rejection must carry a reason** (rule 27): `fn_lc_broadcast_decide` refuses an empty note on the reject path, so the sender always learns what to change.
### Tell residents their room has empty beds, and what it is costing them — Director interview, 2026-08-09
- `supabase/migrations/20260815060001_empty_bed_intimation.sql` — **FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated.** The Director's ask was that "some kind of intimation should be made so that they will actively try to fill up the room"; today nothing tells a learner her room is under-filled and she meets the larger share at billing time, while the invite-a-roommate page has existed for months with **zero invites ever sent**. Adds three global `hostel.empty_bed_notice.*` policy rows — `enabled` seeded **false** as the MASTER SWITCH (the service refuses entirely while it is off; it does not degrade to a dry run), `reminder_interval_days` = 2, and a plain-English `message_template` stating how many beds are empty, the learner's share now, her share if the room fills, and that she can invite someone. Plus the send ledger `hostel_empty_bed_notices`, one row per `(room_id, learner_id, sent_on)`. **`sent_on` is a column, not `sent_at::date`, for two reasons:** a UNIQUE constraint cannot span an expression and only a constraint works as an ON CONFLICT target from PostgREST, and `sent_at::date` resolves in the *session* timezone — a UTC cron between 00:00 and 05:30 IST would bank the notice on yesterday and permit a second one the same Indian morning, so the default is pinned to `Asia/Kolkata`. RLS enabled; anon **and** `authenticated` revoked before the narrow `GRANT SELECT` (a bare grant is a no-op over Supabase's default `GRANT ALL`); read policies only — admin plus `learner_id = auth.uid()` self-read — because the ledger is written exclusively by the service-role cron and a row nobody can forge is the point of the guard. No SECURITY DEFINER function is added. Occupancy is taken from `v_hostel_room_occupancy` (`check_out_date IS NULL`), **not** `actual_vacate_date` — the two "has left" dates have drifted in production before and the bed-uniqueness index reads only the former. Fee figures come from `computeFeeBreakdown` priced twice over one context (today's headcount vs a full room); the formula is not restated anywhere in this change. The migration **reads but does not create** `hostel_room_settle_windows` — that is the sibling settle-bill lane's table, and the service returns a clean no-op with reason `settle_windows_absent` when it is missing, so the two PRs merge in either order. The cron route is **deliberately absent from `vercel.json`**: arming the switch and adding the schedule are two separate decisions, and a schedule added today would start firing the instant the switch flipped with nobody having read a dry run.
### Let the room fill, then bill what is real — settle-then-bill, 2026-08-09
- `supabase/migrations/20260815060000_hostel_settle_then_bill.sql` — **FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated**, and it also ships OFF: `hostel.settle_bill.enabled` seeds `false`, every entry point is inert while it is, and an apply-time assert fails the migration if that switch ever reads true at apply. Adds `hostel_room_settle_windows` (one OPEN window per room per hostel year — the partial unique index COALESCEs a NULL `hostel_year_id` to a sentinel, because Postgres treats NULLs as distinct and a bare pair would allow unlimited open windows on a room whose year is unset), four global policy rows, and eight SECDEF functions, each `SET search_path = public` with EXECUTE revoked from `anon, PUBLIC` and re-granted to `authenticated, service_role` in the same file. Today a learner alone in a 4-bed premium room owes 4× the per-bed rate the moment she moves in and nothing corrects it when roommates arrive; 77 learners currently sit in under-filled rooms with no hostel bill at all.
- 🔓 **A SECURITY DEFINER function bypasses the RLS policies written beside it, so the table's policies were protecting nothing.** The first draft granted the two money-writers to `authenticated` with no guard inside — any logged-in learner in any tenant could have called `fn_settle_bill_close('<any room uuid>', false)` and billed a whole room, or minted credit rows. Every writer now calls `fn_settle_can_manage(room, permission)`, which re-checks the permission AND `role_has_institution_access` on the room's institution; both read lists are scoped through the same helper. The cron bypass is deliberately NARROW: `auth.uid() IS NULL` **alone is not enough** — a token missing `sub`, a psql session holding EXECUTE, pg_cron, or a nested SECURITY DEFINER that reset `request.jwt.claims` would all have landed there and received unconditional cross-tenant write. The session must also carry a `service_role` claim. Proven by negative control: a claimless session and an `authenticated`-claim session both read `can_manage=false`, only `service_role` reads true. If the deployed cron reports some other role this gate refuses it — the correct direction to be wrong in, since the mechanism is OFF and unwired, so a too-tight gate surfaces on the first dry run while a too-loose one is a silent billing hole. **A second apply-time assert greps `pg_get_functiondef` and fails if any writer lacks that call**, so the guard cannot be dropped by a later `CREATE OR REPLACE` without the migration noticing. Proven with a simulated learner session: all three writers raise 42501 and both read lists return 0 rows.
- ⛔ **The parity check is a GATE, not a report — the first draft had it backwards.** `computeFeeBreakdown` is mirrored in SQL (SQL cannot call TS), and `lib/services/campus-living/settle-bill-service.ts` binds the two. Originally it recomputed *after* the live RPC had already INSERTed the bills, so a divergent share would have been billed to real learners and then logged — a post-mortem, not a check. Both money paths now run the dry run FIRST, re-derive every figure through `computeFeeBreakdown` and `remainingWholeMonths`, and only call the live path once the two agree; a mismatch returns `parity_abort` and bills nobody. The SQL returns AC **tonnage and per-month rate**, not just their product, so the re-derivation feeds real inputs instead of reverse-engineering them.
- 💸 **The credit accumulates PER ARRIVAL, and both of its clamps fix a case a simpler formula gets wrong.** Each post-billing arrival contributes `max(0, share(max(n_billed, n_after−1)) − share(max(n_billed, n_after))) × remaining_months(that arrival)/12`, and a resident's entitlement is the sum over every arrival still in the room; each round tops her up toward it. The `max(n_billed, …)` clamp is what makes **departures** behave — a room billed at 2 that loses one resident and gains another still holds 2, so `share(2) − share(2) = 0` and nobody is credited, which is right because she paid for a 2-person room and is in one; two earlier designs (incrementing a stored counter, and reconstructing the step alone) both read that room as "1 → 2" and pay out a half-room credit that was never owed. Summing **per arrival, each with its own month**, is what stops a later arrival in a shorter month from dragging one recomputed target below what was already credited and permanently under-paying the earlier step. With nobody leaving the sum telescopes to `share(n_billed) − share(n_now)`. Measured: departure case → `credits_written 0`; two arrivals → ₹16,667 then a ₹8,333 top-up to ₹25,000, never a second full payment.
- 🧾 **Idempotency is RECORDED, not inferred.** Processed joining events are stamped on the window's `credited_allocation_ids`, whether or not the round wrote a credit row. Inferring it from the existence of credit rows meant any zero-credit round (rounds to 0, every co-resident unbilled) came back forever while the denominator had already advanced. `source_event_id` still carries the joiner's allocation id for the audit trail but is no longer the guard. A partial unique index was considered and rejected: the admission fee-change writer shares `source='fee_structure_change'` and can emit more than one row per learner per event.
- 🔭 **Rule 6 was unreachable from the sweep, so `fn_settle_late_join_due` exists.** Credits were originally driven off `fn_settle_window_due`, which filters `status='open'` — but a late join only matters once the window is `'billed'`, so no cron run would ever have issued one. Proven both ways: the billed room appears in its own due list with `uncredited_joiners 1`, and drops out after the round.
- 🎯 **Other corrections made before merge, each with a concrete failure:** the biller took the OLDEST open window on a room instead of the one it was handed, so a room with windows in two hostel years billed the wrong year at the wrong rate (now accepts `p_window_id`); the hostel-year fallback was `LIMIT 1` with no ORDER BY, and a NULL year would have been stamped onto bills where the dedup key compares `hostel_year_id` — NULL never matches, so that is a **double-bill**, and it now refuses with `no_hostel_year`; the UPDATE policy had `USING` but no `WITH CHECK`, letting a tenant-scoped holder of `campus_living.fees.config` rewrite `room_id` to another institution's room or flip `status` from `billed` back to `open` and clear the double-bill guard.
- 🧬 **Two structural hazards are handled rather than discovered later.** `hostel_allocations.learner_id` FKs `profiles(id)` while `billing_student_bills.student_id` and `student_credit_balances.student_id` FK `learners_profiles(id)`, so every resident is resolved through `profiles.learner_id` and a non-learner resident is reported `not_a_learner` instead of billed. And re-opening a window on an already-billed room would double-bill everyone — nothing at the schema level stops it, since the partial index covers only `status='open'` — so `fn_settle_window_open` refuses and routes to the credit path.
- ⚖️ **Boundaries kept deliberately.** Occupancy is `check_out_date IS NULL` at room level — the exact semantics of `v_hostel_room_occupancy`, which the due list reads rather than recounting; the second "has left" date (`actual_vacate_date`) is NOT consulted, so this can never disagree with the view the rest of campus living bills from. Mess fees are out of scope (flat per learner, not occupancy-sensitive) and stay with `campus_living_generate_hostel_year_bills`, whose dedup key this file now matches exactly (cancelled + superseded) so the two paths can never both bill a room. A room with no category or no active fee row returns `no_rate` and leaves its window OPEN for an admin to fix rather than billing ₹0.
- 🧮 **The TS↔SQL key contract is now proven, because renaming a field on one side silently disabled the whole rule once.** `SettleLateJoinEvent` read `joined_on`/`occupants_before`/`credit_per_resident` while the SQL had been renamed to `anchored_on`/`occupants_at_billing`/`target_per_resident`, so every re-derived figure was `Number(undefined)` = NaN, parity could never hold, and **every live credit round would have returned `parity_abort` — rule 6 could not have written a single credit row.** A SQL-only proof cannot see this; it was found by review and then reproduced by running real `fn_settle_bill_close` / `fn_settle_late_join_credit` dry-run payloads through the shipped TS functions. `verifyLateJoinEvent` is exported for exactly that. The round-trip passes on a live AC payload (₹78,000 → ₹52,000, 10 months, ₹21,667) **and the negative controls fail as they must**: a tampered share is rejected, and so is a missing key — the exact defect. Both parity gates are now fail-CLOSED (anything other than `parity_ok === true` refuses), because they previously passed whenever a primitive was absent.
- 📦 **A learner on a FLAT PACKAGE is skipped, not billed.** Her hostel fee is one bundled package price that does not divide by occupancy, and the generate path keys package bills on `package_id` — so it would never see a `hostel_category` row and would bill her again: a straight double-bill of the room. Detected by asking `campus_living_resolve_hostel_fee` rather than re-deriving its package-matching rules.
- 🚪 **Rules 1–3 have no trigger yet, and that is stated rather than hidden.** Nothing in this PR calls `fn_settle_window_open` — wiring the allocation-create path belongs to the lane that owns allocation, and this PR is forbidden from touching it. Flipping the master switch on today opens zero windows. The mechanism, the policy rows and the sweep all exist and are proven; the hook is the follow-up.
- 🧪 **Proven behaviourally on a throwaway Postgres 16, not by object existence** — switch off → 0 windows and 42501 on a live call; move-in → window open and **0 bills**; joiner → `restart_count` 1; restart capped at `hard_deadline`; dry run → ₹60,000 each (₹30,000/bed × 4 ÷ 2) with **0 rows written and the window still open**; live → 2 bills due in 5 days, re-run `already_billed`; late joiner → no second window, ₹60,000 → ₹40,000, ₹16,667 credited (10 of 12 months), original bills **unchanged**, re-run 0; full room → `room_full`; AC → ₹30,000 + ₹18,000 = ₹48,000. The cron `app/api/cron/campus-living/settle-then-bill` is deliberately absent from `vercel.json` and dry-runs unless `dry_run=false` is passed explicitly.
### Start the settle clock on every move-in, and stop an admin billing another college's rooms — Director interview, 2026-08-10
- `supabase/migrations/20260815070000_settle_window_trigger_and_scope.sql` — **FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated**, and it flips no switch: `hostel.settle_bill.enabled` stays `false` and the same apply-time assert as the engine refuses the file if it ever reads true. Closes the two gaps PR #2954 disclosed about itself. **(1) Nothing started the clock.** No code anywhere called `fn_settle_window_open`, so arming the master switch would have opened **ZERO** windows — measured on a throwaway Postgres 16 against the shipped engine bodies: three move-ins → **0 windows**; with the trigger → **1 window, restart_count 0**. Two AFTER-row triggers on `hostel_allocations` now fire on ARRIVALS ONLY (Director 2026-08-10): the WHEN clauses require `status='active' AND check_out_date IS NULL` **now**, and either that it was not so before or that `room_id` changed — so a departure never even enters the function, because a departure that restarted the clock would postpone the bills of the residents who stayed. Proven: second arrival → `restart_count` 0→1 and the deadline moves, never past `hard_deadline` (with `window_days` forced to 999 the restart clamps **exactly** to the 20-day hard deadline); `check_out_date` set, `status→vacated`, and a routine `fee_status` edit → `restart_count` 2→2 with every deadline unchanged; a move A→B leaves **A's window untouched** and opens B's (then restarts it to 1 on the second mover); `pending_approval→active` is an arrival (2→3), `→suspended` is not (3→3). **AFTER, not BEFORE** — `trg_allocation_guard_reserved_bed` is BEFORE and can reject the row, so these only run on allocations that survived it; they write only `hostel_room_settle_windows`, so there is no re-entry into `hostel_allocations` and no recursion. 🛟 **Placing a learner in a bed outranks opening a billing window** — `fn_settle_window_open` RAISEs 42501 when the writer holds no campus-living permission, and the settle schema may be absent entirely on an environment where the engine has not been applied (both files are Director-gated and may land in either order); an AFTER trigger that raises **aborts the INSERT**, so the call is wrapped in `BEGIN … EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS` (plpgsql's internal savepoint rolls back only the window write) and the failure is surfaced with `RAISE WARNING`, never swallowed silently. Proven both ways, and the swallow is proven **non-vacuous** by a mutant: with the handler removed the identical two writes fail with 42501 and 42883 and **0 rows** are written. SECURITY DEFINER + `SET search_path=public` is load-bearing, not decoration — a plain trigger runs under the writer's own RLS and RLS denial is silent (0 rows, no error), so the window lookup would read nothing and the clock would fail to restart for exactly the callers whose RLS is narrowest; EXECUTE is revoked from `anon, PUBLIC` with no `authenticated` grant, since the triggers are the only caller. **(2) `fn_settle_can_manage` let an admin bill another college's rooms.** It returned true on `is_super_admin() OR is_admin()` **before** it ever read the room's `institution_id`, and every settle writer plus both settle read lists route through that one function — so that branch was the engine's entire cross-tenant surface. Rebuilt VERBATIM from the engine definition with the institution lookup moved above the branch: **45 lines before, 56 after**. `is_super_admin()` keeps unconditional reach and stays above the NULL-room test, so its answer is byte-for-byte unchanged; a plain `is_admin()` must now also satisfy `role_has_institution_access()`. Measured: plain admin of A against a room in B **true → false**, same admin against a room in A **true → true**, super admin against B **true → true**, permission-holder path unchanged, and the deliberately-narrow `service_role` cron bypass **untouched** (service_role claim → true, authenticated claim → false). A fourth apply-time assert greps `pg_get_functiondef` and fails if a later `CREATE OR REPLACE` restores the unscoped branch. All five asserts proven non-vacuous by mutation — restoring the old gate, dropping one trigger, flipping it BEFORE, granting `anon` EXECUTE, and arming the switch each fail the migration by name. The setup files were verified to rebuild the same objects and pass the same asserts. No switch, no cron, no TS, no route, no fee formula.

### Two visitors could still double-book through the 5-minute gap — a padded exclusion constraint (2026-08-13)
- `supabase/migrations/20260830020000_meeting_bookings_padded_gap_exclusion.sql` — **FILE ONLY / NOT APPLIED — Director-gated.** Adds `mb_no_double_booking_padded` ALONGSIDE the live `mb_no_double_booking`, which is left completely untouched. The live constraint excludes on the RAW span (`tstzrange(start_time, end_time)`, read from production 2026-08-13), so it treats 11:00–11:10 and 11:10–11:20 as non-overlapping and accepts both; the 5-minute breathing gap from `20260820000000` is enforced only in the slot engine and on the create path, leaving a TOCTOU window where two simultaneous visitors both pass the application check and both land. The new constraint excludes on the span padded 5 minutes at the START — mirroring the slot engine's own arithmetic (`candStart = start - bufferBefore`, `native-slot-engine.ts:271`), because buffer_BEFORE is what stops a booking butting onto the END of an existing meeting; a gap of exactly 5 minutes is still accepted, 4 is not. ⚠️ **The inline spelling `tstzrange(start_time - interval '5 minutes', end_time)` CANNOT be used** — `timestamptz - interval` is `timestamptz_mi_interval`, marked STABLE (`provolatile='s'`), and Postgres refuses it with `ERROR: functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE` (reproduced on PG 16.14 before the file was written). Hence the tiny helper `public.mb_padded_booking_span(timestamptz, timestamptz)`, whose IMMUTABLE marking is **proven honest rather than asserted**: the same instants reduced by `interval '5 minutes'` across UTC / America/New_York / Europe/Berlin / Asia/Kolkata / Pacific/Chatham over three DST-transition windows give an identical digest (`ed36c0d22676132dd3f063da05020b8c`), while the non-vacuity control `interval '1 day'` gives DIFFERENT digests per zone (UTC `25008308…`, New_York `db8e43a9…`) — so IMMUTABLE would be a lie for a day/month-bearing interval and is true for pure minutes. Scoped by a FIXED literal cutoff of `2026-09-01T00:00Z` because an exclusion constraint cannot be created `NOT VALID` and production holds **14 pairs of confirmed bookings at an exact 0-minute gap (22 distinct rows, one host, all `seat_index` 0, latest 2026-08-08 09:30Z, all already finished)** that would otherwise block creation outright; `now()` is not usable (STABLE → `functions in index predicate must be marked IMMUTABLE`, also reproduced) whereas a timestamptz literal is a parse-time constant and is accepted. 2026-09-01 specifically because **zero bookings of any status start on or after it** (max `start_time` = 2026-08-15 05:35Z), so the constraint validates an empty set and its creation cannot fail however the table drifts before it is applied. 🚨 **Carries an explicit `GRANT EXECUTE … TO anon, authenticated, service_role` that must NOT be "hardened" away** — unlike an RPC, an index-expression function is evaluated during index maintenance on every INSERT: measured on PG 16.14, the default PUBLIC grant lets an insert through, a plain `REVOKE EXECUTE … FROM PUBLIC` makes the identical insert fail with `permission denied for function mb_padded_booking_span`, and the named grant restores it while PUBLIC stays revoked — which matters because this repo sweeps blanket REVOKEs by function name (`20260605191101`, and open PR #3016 does it again). The function is SECURITY INVOKER, reads no table and takes only the two timestamps handed to it, so there is no security cost. Proven behaviourally on a throwaway Postgres 16.14 across 12 steps with the SHIPPED constraint as the control: the racing pair is **accepted** by the live constraint alone (non-vacuity — this IS the bug), then **rejected** with 23P01 once the migration is applied; a 4-minute gap after the cutoff is rejected, an exactly-5-minute gap is accepted, the identical racing pair BEFORE the cutoff is still accepted (this is what protects the 14 historical pairs), group seats 0/1/2 on one slot still coexist, cancelled rows are still ignored, `mb_no_double_booking` still bites on a raw overlap, and a second application is a no-op (`NOTICE: … already present — skipping`) after which the guard still bites. ⚠️⚠️ **THE PREMISE THIS WAS SPECIFIED ON IS FALSE ON PRODUCTION — read before applying.** The work was requested on the understanding that every active meeting type now carries `buffer_before_min = 5`. Measured read-only 2026-08-13: of **252 active `meeting_types`, 199 sit at `buffer_before_min = 0` and only 53 at 5**. That is not drift — `20260820000000` moved the column DEFAULT to 5 and said in its own header that it deliberately did NOT backfill, because doing so "would withdraw slots from 128 host pages that their owners are already offering — a platform-wide behaviour change that was considered and explicitly declined (Director, 2026-08-07)". So for the 53 types at 5 this file closes the race and changes nothing else, but for the other 199 it ALSO imposes a gap their owners never chose, at the one layer the application cannot soften: a legitimate back-to-back booking fails with 23P01 → `SLOT_TAKEN`, telling a visitor the slot is taken seconds after the slot engine offered it. That is the same declined behaviour change arriving through the database instead of through the data.
